1.overview:
Loops are control-flow structures that repeat a block of code while a condition holds (for/while) or for a fixed count (for). Their primary purpose is iteration — executing the same logic multiple times without duplicating source lines. Variable declaration, function definition, and exception handling are separate language features with different roles.

✅ Answer: B — To execute a block of code repeatedly

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. variable declaration happens once with assignment or type declarations; loops consume variables but do not create them as their primary purpose.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. this is the defining behavior of every loop construct — for, while, do-while — in all mainstream languages.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. functions group reusable code; loops call code repeatedly inside an existing block but do not define named callable units.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. try/catch (or try/except) blocks handle runtime errors; loops control repetition, not error recovery.

1.studyTip: Loop = repeat; if = branch; function = reuse; try = errors.

2.overview:
In C, the `/` operator performs integer division when both operands are integers. 5 / 2 discards the fractional part (truncates toward zero), yielding 2 — not 2.5. To get floating-point division you need at least one operand as float/double (e.g., 5.0 / 2). printf("%d", ...) expects an integer format specifier.

✅ Answer: B — 2

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. 2.5 is a floating-point result; integer division in C never produces a float without casting or using float literals.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. integer division 5/2 = 2 with remainder 1 discarded; %d prints 2.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. 3 would require rounding up (ceiling), but C integer division truncates down.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. 0 would imply 2/5 or a modulo confusion, not 5/2.

3.overview:
Python identifier rules: must start with a letter or underscore; may contain letters, digits, and underscores; cannot start with a digit; hyphens and # are operators/syntax, not name characters. variable_1 satisfies all rules.

✅ Answer: B — variable_1

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. identifiers cannot begin with a digit — SyntaxError at parse time.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. starts with letter, contains underscore and digit — fully valid Python name.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. hyphen is the subtraction operator; Python parses this as variable minus 1.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. # starts an inline comment; not part of an identifier.

3.studyTip: Python names: [a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]* — no hyphens, no leading digits.

4.overview:
break immediately terminates the innermost enclosing loop or switch, transferring control to the statement after the loop. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next loop test. They are frequently confused on exams.

✅ Answer: B — Exits the loop entirely

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. that is continue, not break — continue goes to next iteration while staying inside the loop.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. break leaves the loop completely; no further iterations run.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. no standard keyword restarts from iteration 1; you'd reassign counter or use a nested loop structure.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. that describes continue; break exits, not advances.

4.studyTip: break = exit loop; continue = skip to next iteration.

5.overview:
Java constants are declared with final — applied to variables, methods (no override), or classes (no subclass). C/C++ use const; Python has no true const keyword; immutable is a general concept, not a Java keyword.

✅ Answer: B — final

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. static means class-level membership/shared state, not immutability.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. final variable must be assigned once; reference cannot point to new object (object internals may still mutate unless deeply immutable).
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. const is C/C++ keyword; Java uses final instead.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. not a Java keyword — immutability is achieved via final + design (e.g., String class).

5.studyTip: Java constant field: private static final TYPE NAME = value;

6.overview:
Linear search scans each of n elements once in the worst case, comparing the target with every item until found or exhausted. Time complexity is O(n) — linear in input size. O(1) is direct index access; O(log n) is binary search on sorted data; O(n²) is nested loops.

✅ Answer: B — O(n)

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. constant time requires direct addressing (array index, hash lookup average case) — linear search may scan all n elements.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. one pass through up to n elements → linear time.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. logarithmic search halves the search space each step (binary search), not sequential scan.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. quadratic time implies nested iteration over n — not a single linear scan.

6.studyTip: Unsorted search = O(n); sorted array binary search = O(log n).

7.overview:
Conditional execution selects one path based on a Boolean condition. if-else (and switch/match variants) implement branching. Loops repeat; functions organize code; arrays store data.

✅ Answer: C — If-else statement

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. loops repeat while/for a condition; they don't choose between alternate single-pass paths like if-else.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. functions encapsulate code but don't inherently branch — branching uses if inside functions.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. evaluates condition and executes exactly one branch — core conditional construct.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. arrays are data structures for storing multiple values, not control flow.

7.studyTip: Selection (if) vs iteration (loop) vs sequence (statements) — classic control-flow trio.

8.overview:
Python comparison operators return bool. x > 5 is True (10>5) and x < 15 is True (10<15). and requires both True → print outputs True. It does not print the number 10 or raise an error.

✅ Answer: A — True

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. both comparisons hold for x=10, so boolean and is True.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. would require at least one comparison to fail — neither does for x=10.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. print receives a boolean expression result, not the integer x.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. syntax and types are valid; no exception raised.

8.studyTip: Python print(bool_expr) prints True/False, not the original integer.

9.overview:
C primitive types include int, char, float, double, void, etc. string is NOT a built-in primitive — C uses char arrays or char* for text. stdio.h provides string handling via C strings, not a string type.

✅ Answer: C — string

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. int is fundamental numeric primitive in C.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. float is standard floating-point primitive.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. C has no string primitive; text is char[] or pointer to char.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. char stores single character — primitive type.

9.studyTip: C primitives: int, char, float, double. Text = char array.

10.overview:
Modular programming decomposes a large program into smaller modules (functions, classes, files) with clear interfaces. Benefits: easier testing, maintenance, team parallel work, and reuse. It does not eliminate debugging or intentionally slow execution.

✅ Answer: B — To break a program into smaller, manageable functions

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. modularity reduces perceived complexity by separation of concerns — opposite of this answer.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. core definition of modular design — divide and conquer at code level.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. bugs still occur; modules make isolation easier but don't remove debugging.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. modularity may add tiny call overhead but goal is maintainability, not slower execution.

10.studyTip: Modular = smaller units + interfaces; think functions, packages, layers.

11.overview:
Python supports tuple unpacking for simultaneous assignment: a, b = b, a swaps without temp variable by evaluating RHS tuple first then binding names. Arithmetic swap works in some languages but is unnecessary in Python. a=b; b=a fails to swap (loses original a). swap() is not built-in.

✅ Answer: C — a, b = b, a

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. arithmetic swap works in languages without tuple unpacking but is error-prone with overflow; Python idiomatic way is C.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. after first line both hold b's old value — original a is lost.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Python evaluates (b, a) tuple then unpacks — elegant one-line swap.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. no built-in swap(); you'd need a custom function.

11.studyTip: Python swap idiom: a, b = b, a — always remember RHS evaluated first.

12.overview:
Arrays have fixed size (in many languages) and O(1) random access but costly insert/delete in middle. Linked lists allocate nodes dynamically — grow/shrink at runtime without predeclaring max size. Access is O(n) for linked lists; memory overhead per node exists.

✅ Answer: B — Dynamic size adjustment

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. arrays offer O(1) index access; linked lists require O(n) traversal.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. linked lists allocate nodes as needed — primary advantage over static arrays.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. linked lists store pointer overhead per node — often MORE memory.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. insertion is O(1) only at known position with pointer; searching that position is still O(n).

12.studyTip: Linked list wins on dynamic size; array wins on random access.

13.overview:
Stack: Last-In-First-Out — push adds to top, pop removes top (like plate stack). Queue: FIFO — first in, first out. Linked list is implementation structure; binary tree is hierarchical.

✅ Answer: B — Stack

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. queue is FIFO — opposite order of LIFO.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. LIFO defines stack behavior — used in call stacks, undo, parsing.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. linked list is implementation technique; LIFO describes stack ADT.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. tree organizes hierarchical data with left/right children, not LIFO.

13.studyTip: LIFO = Stack; FIFO = Queue — memorize both acronyms.

14.overview:
QuickSort average O(n log n) but worst case O(n²) when pivots are poorly chosen (already sorted with first-element pivot). MergeSort guarantees O(n log n) worst case. Exam asks worst case.

✅ Answer: B — O(n²)

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. average/good-case QuickSort, not worst case.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. worst case with unbalanced partitions — all elements on one side of pivot.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. linear time is one pass — QuickSort is divide-and-conquer with recursion.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. logarithmic is binary search style, not sorting entire array.

14.studyTip: QuickSort worst = O(n²); MergeSort worst = O(n log n).

15.overview:
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source to all vertices in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights. DFS/BFS don't handle weighted shortest path optimally. Merge Sort sorts arrays.

✅ Answer: C — Dijkstra's Algorithm

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. DFS explores deeply — doesn't guarantee shortest weighted path.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graphs, not weighted.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. classic greedy algorithm for non-negative weighted shortest paths.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. sorting algorithm, unrelated to graph pathfinding.

15.studyTip: Weighted shortest path (non-negative) → Dijkstra; unweighted → BFS.

16.overview:
Binary Search Tree property: for every node, all keys in left subtree are less than node's key; all keys in right subtree are greater (or equal depending on variant). Less-than values go LEFT of root.

✅ Answer: B — Left subtree

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. right subtree holds values GREATER than root.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. BST invariant: left < root < right.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. parent is one level up — not where all smaller values live.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. root is single comparison point; smaller values descend left.

16.studyTip: BST: left smaller, right larger — trace insertions on paper.

17.overview:
Balanced BST (AVL, Red-Black) maintains height O(log n), so insert/search/delete are O(log n). Unbalanced degenerate tree can be O(n). Balanced guarantees logarithmic height.

✅ Answer: C — O(log n)

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. insertion must traverse tree height — cannot be constant for arbitrary size.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. would be skewed/unbalanced tree worst case, not balanced BST.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. balanced tree height ~ log n → insert takes proportional steps.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. no standard BST operation is quadratic for single insert.

17.studyTip: Balanced BST operations: O(log n); skewed chain: O(n).

18.overview:
Inheritance allows subclass (derived) to acquire fields and methods from superclass (base). Encapsulation hides internals; polymorphism is many forms; abstraction hides complexity.

✅ Answer: C — Inheritance

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. bundling data + methods with access control — not parent-child sharing.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. same interface, different behavior — often uses inheritance but is distinct principle.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. is-a relationship: Dog extends Animal inherits sound(), etc.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. showing essential features while hiding detail — broader design concept.

18.studyTip: Four OOP pillars: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism.

19.overview:
Encapsulation restricts direct access to internal state via private fields and public getters/setters. Goal: protect invariants, reduce coupling, allow implementation change without breaking clients.

✅ Answer: B — To hide data and restrict direct access

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Java allows one class inheritance; multiple inheritance is separate language feature, not encapsulation's purpose.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. private/protected modifiers + accessors = encapsulation.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. overloading is compile-time polymorphism — same name, different parameters.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. abstract classes support inheritance/abstraction, not primarily data hiding definition.

19.studyTip: Encapsulation = data hiding + controlled access through methods.

20.overview:
Java this refers to current object instance — access instance fields, call other constructors (this()), pass current object. super refers to parent class. self is Python. instance is not keyword.

✅ Answer: A — this

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. this.field, this.method(), this() constructor chaining.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. super accesses superclass members — different from current object reference.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Python convention for instance reference; Java uses this.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. not a Java keyword for current object.

21.overview:
Runtime polymorphism: Animal reference holds Dog object; overridden sound() in Dog is invoked via dynamic dispatch (virtual method table). Static type is Animal; dynamic type is Dog — Bark prints.

✅ Answer: B — Bark

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. would be result if sound() were not overridden or reference called static binding on non-virtual method.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. method overriding + dynamic dispatch → Dog.sound() runs.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. valid Java — subclass IS-A superclass; assignment legal.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. sound() explicitly prints Bark.

21.studyTip: Override + parent reference to child object → child method runs (dynamic binding).

22.overview:
Polymorphism ('many forms'): same method name, different behavior in subclasses via overriding, or overloading at compile time. Overriding subclass method is classic polymorphism example.

✅ Answer: B — Overriding a method in a subclass

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. basic syntax — not polymorphism.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. runtime polymorphism through method override.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. final const declaration — unrelated.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. control flow — not OOP polymorphism.

23.overview:
HTML anchor element <a href="url"> creates clickable hyperlinks. <link> is for external resources (CSS) in head. <href> and <url> are not valid HTML tags.

✅ Answer: B — <a>

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. link associates document with stylesheet/icon — not inline hyperlinks.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. anchor tag with href attribute defines hyperlinks.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. not an HTML element — href is an attribute name.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. not standard HTML tag.

24.overview:
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls presentation: colors, fonts, layout, spacing, responsive design. HTML structures content; JavaScript adds behavior; server-side code handles business logic.

✅ Answer: B — To style and format web pages

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. PHP, Java servlets, Node handle server logic — not CSS.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. CSS separates presentation from HTML structure.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. DBMS/SQL layer — unrelated to CSS.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. browser executes JS; CSS is declarative styling rules.

24.studyTip: HTML=structure, CSS=presentation, JS=behavior — separation of concerns.

25.overview:
JavaScript array methods: push() adds to end; pop() removes from end; shift() removes from front; unshift() adds to front. push/end pair is most commonly tested.

✅ Answer: A — push()

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. arr.push(item) appends to end, returns new length.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. removes and returns LAST element — opposite of add.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. removes FIRST element.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. adds to beginning, not end.

26.overview:
AJAX = Asynchronous JavaScript and XML — technique for background server communication without full page reload. Modern apps often use JSON instead of XML but acronym remains.

✅ Answer: A — Asynchronous JavaScript and XML

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. correct expansion — async partial updates.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Active is wrong first word — Asynchronous.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. JSON not in original acronym expansion.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Automated and XHTML are incorrect.

26.studyTip: AJAX enables fetch/XHR calls updating page sections dynamically.

27.overview:
HTTP GET requests retrieve/read resources — idempotent, parameters often in URL query string. POST creates/submits data; PUT updates; DELETE removes.

✅ Answer: B — GET

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. POST submits entity body — typically create or non-idempotent actions.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. retrieve data from server — read operation.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. replace/update resource at URI.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. remove resource.

28.overview:
Classic JavaScript runs in the browser (client-side) interpreting HTML/CSS DOM. Node.js enables server-side JS but exam default context is browser client execution.

✅ Answer: B — Client-side

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. server-side JS exists (Node) but traditional web JS is client-side.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. browser executes JS embedded or linked from HTML.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. databases run SQL/stored procedures — not JS engine primary role.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. middleware sits between client/server — not primary JS execution context.

28.studyTip: Browser JS manipulates DOM; server logic often PHP/Java/Python/Node.

29.overview:
Postfix x++ uses 5 then increments to 6. Prefix ++x increments first. Expression: x++ + ++x → 5 + 6 = 11? Wait: after x++ x becomes 6, ++x makes x=7 and uses 7? Trace: x=5; left x++ returns 5, x=6; ++x returns 7, x=7; 5+7=12. Answer is 12.

✅ Answer: C — 12

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. would be 5+5 without prefix increment on second operand.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. common miscalculation ignoring that ++x increments before use.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. x++ yields 5; ++x yields 7; sum = 12.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. over-counts increment steps.

29.studyTip: Trace increment operators left-to-right: postfix returns old, prefix returns new.

30.overview:
PHP is widely taught as server-side scripting for web (WordPress, legacy apps). HTML/CSS are markup/style; JavaScript primarily client (though Node exists).

✅ Answer: C — PHP

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. markup language — not scripting.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. stylesheet — not server scripting.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. runs on server, generates HTML dynamically.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. primarily client-side in browser context of exam.

30.studyTip: Server-side scripting examples: PHP, Python/Django, Java/JSP, Node.js.

31.overview:
Django is Python web framework providing MVC/MVT structure, ORM, routing, templates, admin — full scaffolding for web apps, not just database or styling.

✅ Answer: B — To provide a structure for developing web applications

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. ORM is part of Django but framework scope is broader.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. routing, views, templates, models.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. CSS handles styling; Django is server-side.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. ORM abstracts SQL; not raw query executor only.

31.studyTip: Frameworks (Django, Spring, Rails) = structure + conventions + built-in tools.

32.overview:
Android traditionally used Java (now Kotlin preferred officially). Swift is iOS. Python/C++ are not primary Android app languages.

✅ Answer: B — Java

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Apple iOS/macOS language — not Android.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. long-standing primary Android SDK language alongside Kotlin.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. not native Android UI development language.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. used in NDK/native code but not primary app language.

32.studyTip: Android: Java/Kotlin + XML layouts; iOS: Swift/Objective-C.

33.overview:
Activity represents single screen with UI and lifecycle (onCreate, onPause, etc.). Service runs background; BroadcastReceiver handles events; ContentProvider shares data.

✅ Answer: A — Activity

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. screen + user interaction — defines UI for one focused task.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. long-running background work without UI.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. responds to system/app broadcasts.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. structured data sharing between apps.

33.studyTip: Activity = screen; Service = background; Intent = messaging.

34.overview:
Intent is messaging object for starting activities, services, delivering broadcasts — carries action, data URI, extras between components.

✅ Answer: B — To facilitate communication between components

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Room/SQLite handle persistence — not Intent purpose.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. explicit/implicit intents link app parts.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Service component handles background; Intent starts it.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. permissions/Manifest secure app — not Intent role.

34.studyTip: Intent = navigation + data passing between Android components.

35.overview:
AndroidManifest.xml declares app components, permissions, intent filters, package name, min SDK — required app metadata file.

✅ Answer: A — AndroidManifest.xml

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. permissions like INTERNET, CAMERA declared here.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. build dependencies and SDK versions — not runtime permissions list.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. layout UI definition for one screen.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Activity logic source — permissions not declared in Java file.

36.overview:
Mobile security requires encrypting sensitive data at rest (SharedPreferences, SQLite) and in transit (TLS). Storing passwords/API keys plaintext is critical vulnerability.

✅ Answer: B — Storing sensitive data unencrypted

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. UX choice — not security vulnerability.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. data breach if device compromised — major OWASP mobile risk.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. performance/storage concern — not primary security issue.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. normal architecture — not security flaw.

36.studyTip: Mobile security: encrypt secrets, use KeyStore, HTTPS, certificate pinning.

37.overview:
Primary key uniquely identifies each row — NOT NULL + UNIQUE. Enables relationships via foreign keys and efficient indexing.

✅ Answer: B — To uniquely identify each record

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. primary key FORBIDS duplicates — opposite.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. exact definition of primary key constraint.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. foreign keys live in child table referencing parent's PK.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. PK creates index on key column(s) only — not every column.

37.studyTip: PK = unique + not null identifier per row.

38.overview:
SQL DML: INSERT adds rows; UPDATE modifies existing rows; DELETE removes; SELECT queries.

✅ Answer: B — UPDATE

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. adds new records — doesn't modify existing.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. SET column= value WHERE condition modifies existing data.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. removes rows — doesn't change remaining row values.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. read-only retrieval — no modification.

39.overview:
WHERE Age > 20 filters rows strictly greater than 20 — relational comparison on Age column.

✅ Answer: B — Records from Students where Age is greater than 20

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. no filter would need SELECT * FROM Students without WHERE.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. matches SQL predicate exactly.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. would be Age < 20 — wrong operator.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. returns empty only if no rows satisfy condition — not definition.

39.studyTip: Read WHERE clause literally: > means greater than.

40.overview:
Normalization decomposes tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies (insert/delete/update). Goals: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF — organized data without unnecessary duplication.

✅ Answer: B — Organizing data to eliminate redundancy

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. denormalization adds redundancy — opposite of normalization.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. core purpose of normalization process.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. normalization works within schema design — not multi-DB creation.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. may happen during redesign but not definition of normalization.

40.studyTip: Normalization removes redundancy; denormalization adds it for performance.

41.overview:
One-to-Many: one parent row relates to many child rows via FK in child table (one Department, many Employees). One-to-One is rare; Many-to-Many needs junction table.

✅ Answer: B — One-to-Many

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. each parent maps to exactly one child — stricter than PK-FK typical pattern.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. classic PK in parent, FK in child referencing it.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. requires associative/junction table with two FKs.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. FK explicitly defines relationship.

41.studyTip: PK→FK pattern usually One-to-Many (one customer, many orders).

42.overview:
ACID transaction properties: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed survives crash).

✅ Answer: A — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. canonical database transaction acronym.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. plausible words but not ACID expansion.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. wrong first letters — not ACID.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Integration is wrong third word.

42.studyTip: ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — memorize exactly.

43.overview:
Operating system manages CPU, memory, I/O devices, file systems; provides abstraction and scheduling for applications. It doesn't write app code or compile programs (compiler tool job).

✅ Answer: B — To manage hardware and software resources

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. developers write applications; OS provides platform.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. core OS definition — resource manager.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. UI design is application/GUI toolkit layer.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. compiler is separate utility (gcc, javac) — OS may invoke it.

43.studyTip: OS = resource manager + abstraction layer between hardware and apps.

44.overview:
Shortest Job Next (SJN) / Shortest Remaining Time First picks process with smallest next CPU burst. FCFS is arrival order; Round Robin uses time quantum; Priority uses priority field.

✅ Answer: B — Shortest Job Next

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. FIFO queue — ignores burst length.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. selects shortest next CPU burst — minimizes average wait in theory.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. time-sliced fair scheduling with quantum.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. uses priority values, not strictly shortest burst.

44.studyTip: Shortest burst → SJN/SRTF; time quantum → Round Robin.

45.overview:
Deadlock: circular wait — each process holds resource another needs, none can proceed. Requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait (Coffman conditions).

✅ Answer: B — A situation where processes are unable to proceed due to resource conflicts

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. infinite loop — not deadlock (no resource circular wait).
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. classic deadlock definition.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. may kill process but not mutual blocking deadlock.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. physical fault — unrelated to resource deadlock.

45.studyTip: Deadlock = circular wait for resources; prevention/avoidance/detection strategies exist.

46.overview:
Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size frames; logical memory into same-size pages. Segmentation uses variable-sized logical segments. Swapping moves processes in/out of memory.

✅ Answer: A — Paging

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. fixed-size partitions (frames/pages) — answer.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. variable-sized segments reflecting logical program parts.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. moves entire processes between disk and memory.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. problem (external/internal), not management technique.

46.studyTip: Paging = fixed size; Segmentation = variable size; both map virtual→physical.

47.overview:
Mutex (mutual exclusion lock) ensures only one thread/process enters critical section at a time, preventing race conditions on shared data.

✅ Answer: B — To ensure mutual exclusion

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. malloc/allocator handles memory — not mutex.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. lock before critical section, unlock after.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. scheduler picks next process — different subsystem.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. device drivers/I/O subsystem — not mutex role.

48.overview:
Modern OS security: user authentication, access control lists, ASLR, DEP, encryption, mandatory access control. Plaintext passwords and disabling firewalls are anti-patterns.

✅ Answer: B — Implementing user authentication

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. violates least privilege — security failure.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. verify identity before granting access — valid control.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. weakens network protection — bad practice.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. critical vulnerability — never acceptable.

48.studyTip: OS security: authentication, authorization, auditing, encryption.

49.overview:
Software engineering applies systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approaches to develop reliable, efficient, maintainable software — not increasing complexity or skipping testing.

✅ Answer: B — To develop reliable and efficient software systems

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. goal is manage complexity, not increase it.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. IEEE/SWEBOK aligned primary goal.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. appropriate documentation is essential deliverable.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. testing is integral to quality assurance.

49.studyTip: SE = systematic development of quality software within constraints.

50.overview:
Waterfall model: requirements → design → implementation → testing → maintenance in strict sequential phases with phase gates. Agile/Scrum are iterative; Spiral is risk-driven cycles.

✅ Answer: B — Waterfall

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. iterative, adaptive — opposite of strict linear sequence.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. linear sequential SDLC model.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. iterative with explicit risk analysis loops.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. agile framework with sprints — not linear waterfall.

50.studyTip: Waterfall = sequential phases; Agile = iterative delivery.

51.overview:
Agile emphasizes iterative/incremental delivery, customer collaboration, responding to change. Fixed requirements and no user involvement contradict Agile Manifesto values.

✅ Answer: B — Iterative and incremental development

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Agile expects evolving requirements.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. short cycles delivering working software.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Agile requires continuous stakeholder/customer feedback.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. multiple iterations/sprints — not one phase.

51.studyTip: Agile Manifesto: individuals, working software, collaboration, responding to change.

52.overview:
UML dynamic behavior diagrams: Sequence (message order over time), Activity (workflow), State Machine (state transitions). Class/Component are structural.

✅ Answer: C — Sequence Diagram

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. static structure — classes, attributes, relationships.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. actor-system interactions — behavioral at use-case level.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. shows object interactions over time — dynamic behavior.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. physical/software components and dependencies — structural.

52.studyTip: Dynamic: Sequence, Activity, State. Static: Class, Component, Deployment.

53.overview:
Feasibility study evaluates technical, economic, operational, schedule viability before committing resources — answers 'should we proceed?' not how to code.

✅ Answer: B — To assess the viability of a project

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. implementation phase activity.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. technical/economic/operational feasibility analysis.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. deployment is late SDLC stage.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. verification/validation — separate phase.

53.studyTip: Feasibility = can/should we build it? (TEOS: Technical, Economic, Operational, Schedule).

54.overview:
Non-functional requirements (NFRs) specify quality constraints: performance, security, usability, reliability. Login, store data, generate reports are functional capabilities.

✅ Answer: B — The system must respond within 2 seconds

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. functional — describes a system capability.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. performance NFR — measurable quality constraint.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. functional data storage requirement.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. functional feature requirement.

54.studyTip: Functional = what system does; Non-functional = how well (quality attributes).

55.overview:
Requirements elicitation discovers stakeholder needs through interviews, workshops, observation, prototypes — before design and coding.

✅ Answer: B — To gather and document user needs

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. testing validates built product — post-implementation.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. elicitation = extract and record requirements.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. release to production — far downstream.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. implementation follows requirements specification.

55.studyTip: Elicitation techniques: interviews, surveys, observation, prototyping, document analysis.

56.overview:
Stakeholder interviews are classic requirements gathering technique — direct conversation to uncover needs, constraints, and priorities.

✅ Answer: B — Conducting interviews

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. implementation — not requirements gathering.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. structured/unstructured interviews with stakeholders.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. fixing defects in existing code.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. release activity — not elicitation.

56.studyTip: Requirements gathering: interviews, JAD sessions, questionnaires, ethnography.

57.overview:
Testable requirement is unambiguous, measurable, verifiable with clear acceptance criteria. 'System shall respond within 2 seconds under 100 concurrent users' is testable; 'system shall be fast' is not.

✅ Answer: B — It is measurable and verifiable

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. vague requirements are NOT testable.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. can write test cases with pass/fail criteria.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. lack of clarity prevents testing.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. incomplete requirements hinder verification.

57.studyTip: SMART requirements: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

58.overview:
Software Requirements Specification (SRS) documents functional and non-functional requirements, interfaces, constraints — contract between stakeholders and developers.

✅ Answer: B — Software Requirements Specification (SRS)

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. SDD describes HOW — architecture and design, not full requirements.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. WHAT the system must do and quality constraints.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. how testing will be conducted — derived from requirements.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. end-user guide for operating finished system.

58.studyTip: SRS = requirements; SDD = design; Test Plan = verification strategy.

59.overview:
Requirements change during development (scope creep, new regulations, market shifts) is primary management challenge — needs traceability and change control.

✅ Answer: B — Handling requirement changes during development

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. coding challenge — not requirements management focus.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. change impact analysis and version control.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. deployment challenge — different domain.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. UI testing — not requirements management core issue.

59.studyTip: Requirements volatility → change control boards, traceability matrices, agile backlogs.

60.overview:
Software architecture defines high-level structure (components, connectors), behavior, and quality attribute tradeoffs — blueprint before detailed coding.

✅ Answer: B — To define the system's structure and behavior

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. implementation follows architecture.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. components, interactions, constraints.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. QA activity — separate from architectural definition.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. operations/release management.

60.studyTip: Architecture = structures + behaviors + quality attribute rationale.

61.overview:
Bridge pattern decouples abstraction from implementation so both can vary independently (e.g., Shape abstraction with different Renderer implementations). Singleton ensures one instance; Factory creates objects; Observer notifies dependents.

✅ Answer: C — Bridge

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. ensures single instance — creational pattern, not abstraction/implementation split.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. creates objects without specifying exact class — creational.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. separates interface/abstraction from implementation hierarchy.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. publish-subscribe notification — behavioral pattern.

61.studyTip: Bridge = abstraction vs implementation; Adapter = interface conversion.

62.overview:
Client-Server architecture: clients request services; servers provide resources — fundamental web model (browser/server). Monolithic is single deployable; Pipe-and-Filter streams data; Layered organizes tiers.

✅ Answer: B — Client-Server

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. single unified application — can host web but exam targets distributed web model.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. browsers/clients communicate with web servers — standard web architecture.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. data processing pipeline — Unix filters, compilers — not typical web label.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. organizes tiers (presentation/business/data) — can be inside client-server but Client-Server is the web-appropriate architectural style asked.

62.studyTip: Web apps: Client-Server with possible Layered or MVC inside server.

63.overview:
Quality attributes (non-functional): performance, scalability, availability, security, modifiability. Programming language and team size are project context, not architecture quality attributes.

✅ Answer: B — The system's performance or scalability

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. technology choice — not ISO 25010 quality attribute.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. classic architectural quality attribute.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. project staffing — not system quality attribute.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. management constraint — not architecture quality attribute.

63.studyTip: Quality attributes: -ility words (availability, scalability, modifiability, usability).

64.overview:
Class Diagram shows static structure: classes, attributes, methods, relationships (inheritance, association). Sequence/Activity are behavioral; Use Case shows actor interactions.

✅ Answer: B — Class Diagram

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. message passing over time — dynamic behavior.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. structural view of system classes and relationships.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. workflow/process flow — behavioral.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. actors and use cases — functional scope, not class structure.

65.overview:
Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) hierarchically decomposes project deliverables into work packages — foundation for scheduling, estimating, assigning responsibility.

✅ Answer: B — To divide a project into manageable tasks

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. development task — not WBS purpose.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. decomposition of scope into work packages.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. QA activity.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. release/operations activity.

65.studyTip: WBS: 100% rule — sum of work packages equals total project scope.

66.overview:
Gantt chart visualizes tasks on timeline with bars showing duration and dependencies — standard PM scheduling tool.

✅ Answer: A — Gantt Chart

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. task bars, milestones, dependencies over calendar time.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. proportions of whole — not schedule visualization.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. frequency distribution — statistics, not project scheduling.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. correlation between variables — not task dependencies.

66.studyTip: Gantt = schedule; PERT = network diagram; both used in project time management.

67.overview:
Risk management: identify, analyze, prioritize, plan responses (mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept), monitor throughout project lifecycle.

✅ Answer: B — Identifying and mitigating potential risks

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. implementation — not risk management.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. core risk management cycle.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. UX design activity.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. QA/data validation activity.

67.studyTip: Risk response: avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept (AMTA mnemonic).

68.overview:
Product Owner owns product backlog, prioritizes user stories by business value, represents stakeholders. Scrum Master facilitates process; Dev Team builds; stakeholders advise.

✅ Answer: B — Product Owner

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. removes impediments, coaches process — doesn't prioritize backlog.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. single person accountable for backlog ordering and value.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. implements items — may estimate but PO prioritizes.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. provide input but PO makes prioritization decisions.

69.overview:
Project schedule plans task start/finish dates, milestones, critical path — tracks progress against baseline timeline.

✅ Answer: B — To plan and track project timelines

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. code documentation — developer activity.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. schedule management purpose.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. QA — separate from scheduling.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. infrastructure — not schedule primary focus.

69.studyTip: Schedule baseline + Gantt/PERT + critical path method (CPM).

70.overview:
Unit testing verifies smallest testable units (functions, methods, classes) in isolation, often with mocks/stubs. Integration/system/UI tests cover broader scope.

✅ Answer: B — To test individual components or functions

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. system testing — whole integrated product.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. unit test definition.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. UI/acceptance testing domain.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. database testing specific layer.

70.studyTip: Test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration, fewest E2E/system.

71.overview:
White-box (structural) testing uses internal code structure — branches, paths, statements. Black-box tests I/O without knowing internals. Integration/system are levels, not techniques by structure.

✅ Answer: B — White-box testing

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. tests external behavior without code knowledge.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. uses code structure for coverage (branch, path).
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. tests combined modules — test level, not structural technique.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. whole system validation — test level.

71.studyTip: White-box = see code (coverage); Black-box = see inputs/outputs only.

72.overview:
Test case specifies inputs, execution conditions, expected results to verify specific requirement or behavior — fundamental QA artifact.

✅ Answer: A — A set of conditions to verify a system's functionality

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. test case definition.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. test script automates cases but case is logical specification.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. PM document — different purpose.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. data model — not test case.

72.studyTip: Test case = preconditions + inputs + expected result + postconditions.

73.overview:
Quality Assurance ensures processes and products meet specified requirements and standards — prevent defects through process, not just find them (QC/testing).

✅ Answer: B — To ensure the software meets specified requirements

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. QA aims for efficiency with quality — not lengthen arbitrarily.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. conformance to specs and standards.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. QA often requires documented processes (ISO, CMMI).
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. user feedback essential for quality improvement.

73.studyTip: QA = process focus; QC/Testing = product verification.

74.overview:
Software defect (bug) is behavior deviating from specified requirements — causes incorrect results or crashes. Features meeting requirements are not defects.

✅ Answer: B — A bug that causes incorrect behavior

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. correct behavior — not a defect.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. failure to meet specification — defect.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. good practice — not defect.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. deliverable documentation — not defect.

74.studyTip: Defect = gap between expected (spec) and actual (behavior).

75.overview:
Software maintenance modifies deployed software after delivery — corrective, adaptive, perfective, preventive — not greenfield development.

✅ Answer: B — Updating and fixing existing software

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. new development — not maintenance.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. maintenance definition per IEEE.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. could be part of perfective maintenance but too narrow.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. release activity — maintenance follows deployment.

75.studyTip: Maintenance types: Corrective, Adaptive, Perfective, Preventive (CAPP).

76.overview:
Corrective maintenance fixes reported bugs/errors after release. Adaptive adapts to environment changes; perfective improves performance/features; preventive prevents future issues.

✅ Answer: A — Corrective maintenance

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. fixes user-reported faults — answer.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. adjusts to OS/hardware/regulatory environment changes.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. enhancements and performance improvements.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. refactoring to reduce future failure risk.

76.studyTip: User bug report → Corrective; OS upgrade compatibility → Adaptive.

77.overview:
Refactoring improves internal code structure (readability, design patterns) without changing external observable behavior — key maintenance discipline.

✅ Answer: B — Improving code structure without changing functionality

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. perfective enhancement — changes functionality.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. refactoring definition (Fowler).
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. may happen during refactor but not the definition.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. verification activity — not refactoring.

77.studyTip: Refactor = same behavior, better structure; feature = new behavior.

78.overview:
Maintenance cost correlates strongly with system complexity — tangled code, poor documentation, high coupling increase change cost (Lehman's laws).

✅ Answer: C — The complexity of the software

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. minor factor compared to complexity and design quality.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. may affect adaptive load but not primary cost driver in SE theory.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. complex systems cost more to understand and modify.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. schedule pressure affects cost but complexity is structural driver.

78.studyTip: Lehman's Law: complexity increases unless work done to reduce it.

79.overview:
Best practices (code reviews, testing, documentation, refactoring) improve reliability and reduce defect rates over system lifetime.

✅ Answer: B — Improved software reliability

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. best practices reduce bugs — opposite.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. primary long-term benefit of maintenance discipline.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. good maintenance includes adequate docs.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. initial investment pays off in lower maintenance cost.

79.studyTip: Invest in maintainability early — majority of cost is post-release maintenance.

80.overview:
OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model standardizes networking into 7 layers — interoperability reference model, not a protocol itself or hardware manager.

✅ Answer: B — To standardize network communication layers

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. protocols implement layers — OSI is reference framework.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. 7-layer conceptual model for teaching/design.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. OS role — OSI is network-specific.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. security spans layers but OSI primary purpose is layering standard.

80.studyTip: OSI 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

81.overview:
Network layer (Layer 3) handles logical addressing (IP) and routing packets across networks. Data Link (L2) uses MAC/switching; Transport (L4) TCP/UDP; Application (L7) HTTP/DNS.

✅ Answer: B — Network Layer

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. MAC addresses, switches, frames — local segment.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. IP routing between networks — routers operate here.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. end-to-end segments, TCP/UDP ports.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. user-facing protocols HTTP, FTP, SMTP.

81.studyTip: Router = Layer 3; Switch = Layer 2; HTTP = Layer 7.

82.overview:
Router forwards IP packets between different networks using routing tables — connects LANs to WANs. Switch connects devices same LAN; doesn't store packets long-term.

✅ Answer: B — To forward data packets between networks

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. switch/hub role on same broadcast domain.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. router interconnects distinct IP networks.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. routers forward — buffering temporary, not storage purpose.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. VPN appliances may encrypt; basic routing doesn't require encryption.

82.studyTip: Switch = same network; Router = between networks; Gateway = protocol translation.

83.overview:
HTTPS = HTTP over TLS/SSL — encrypts web traffic, authenticates server via certificates. HTTP is plaintext; FTP file transfer; SMTP email.

✅ Answer: C — HTTPS

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. unencrypted web protocol — not secure.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. file transfer protocol — not primary secure web browsing.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. HTTP Secure — TLS encryption for web communication.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — email, not web browsing security.

83.studyTip: Secure web = HTTPS (port 443); plain HTTP = port 80.

84.overview:
Subnet mask defines network vs host portion of IP address, enabling subnet division and routing decisions — not encryption or DHCP assignment directly.

✅ Answer: B — To divide a network into smaller subnetworks

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. encryption uses TLS/IPsec — not subnet mask function.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. subnetting splits address space logically.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. DHCP assigns; mask defines subnet boundaries.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. ACLs/firewalls secure; mask defines topology.

84.studyTip: Subnet mask + IP = network address + host address (AND operation).

85.overview:
Gateway connects networks using different protocols or architectures — translates between them (e.g., IP to legacy system). Switch/hub same protocol L2; repeater amplifies signal.

✅ Answer: C — Gateway

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. L2 device forwarding frames within same network technology.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. L1 broadcast device — deprecated, no intelligence.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. interconnects heterogeneous networks with protocol translation.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. regenerates signal on same segment — extends distance only.

85.studyTip: Gateway = different network types; Router = different IP subnets same stack.

86.overview:
Encryption transforms plaintext to ciphertext using keys — protects confidentiality so unauthorized parties cannot read data. Does not primarily speed up or simplify code.

✅ Answer: B — To protect data confidentiality

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. ciphertext may be larger but that's side effect, not purpose.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. core goal of encryption in CIA triad.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. encryption adds computational overhead — slows, not speeds.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. crypto adds complexity — libraries help but not simplification goal.

87.overview:
SQL Injection inserts malicious SQL through unsanitized user input in web forms/queries — OWASP Top 10 vulnerability. Phishing is social engineering; DoS floods resources; brute force guesses passwords.

✅ Answer: B — SQL Injection

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. deceptive emails/sites stealing credentials — social attack.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. malicious SQL in input fields exploiting dynamic query construction.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. overwhelms availability — not code injection into DB queries.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. systematic password guessing — not SQL code injection.

87.studyTip: Prevent SQLi: parameterized queries/prepared statements, input validation, least privilege DB accounts.

88.overview:
Firewall monitors/filters network traffic based on rules (IP, port, protocol) — perimeter defense between trusted/untrusted networks.

✅ Answer: B — To monitor and control network traffic

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. storage devices/servers store — firewall filters traffic.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. allow/deny rules at network boundary.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. DHCP server assigns IP addresses.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. DBMS manages data — unrelated to firewall.

88.studyTip: Firewall + IDS/IPS = network security monitoring and control.

89.overview:
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) requires two or more factors: something you know (password), have (token/phone), are (biometric). SSO is single login for multiple apps — different concept.

✅ Answer: B — Multi-Factor Authentication

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. one login accesses multiple services — convenience, not multi-factor.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. combines independent authentication factors.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. single factor only — something you know.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. one factor (something you have) unless combined with password.

89.studyTip: MFA = 2+ factors; examples: password + SMS OTP, password + fingerprint.

90.overview:
Regular security patches fix known vulnerabilities (CVEs) — critical mitigation. Ignoring feedback, increasing complexity, disabling encryption worsen security posture.

✅ Answer: B — Applying regular security patches

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. bad practice — doesn't mitigate vulnerabilities.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. closes known exploits — essential hygiene.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. more complexity often means more attack surface.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. removes confidentiality protection — dangerous.

90.studyTip: Patch management: test patches, deploy promptly, monitor CVE advisories.

91.overview:
Intelligent agent (Russell & Norvig): entity that perceives environment through sensors and acts through actuators to achieve goals — foundational AI concept.

✅ Answer: B — A system that perceives and acts in an environment

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. code generation tool — not agent definition.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. canonical agent definition.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. stores data — no perception/action loop.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. UI presents information — agent includes reasoning/action.

91.studyTip: Agent = Perceive + Act + (optional) Learn in Environment.

92.overview:
Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores all nodes at depth d before depth d+1 — level-order, uses queue. DFS goes deep first (stack); A*/Greedy use heuristics.

✅ Answer: B — Breadth-First Search

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. explores one branch deeply before backtracking — not level-by-level.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. expands shallowest nodes first — current depth before deeper.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. informed best-first with f(n)=g(n)+h(n) — not strictly level-order.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. uses heuristic only — may not explore all nodes at current depth.

92.studyTip: BFS = queue, level-order; DFS = stack, depth-first; BFS finds shortest path unweighted.

93.overview:
Expert system knowledge base stores domain facts and IF-THEN rules for inference engine to reason and explain decisions — distinct from user data storage.

✅ Answer: B — To store rules and facts for decision-making

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. user profiles are application data — not knowledge base purpose.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. domain knowledge + production rules.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. OS responsibility — not expert system KB.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. inference engine uses KB; KB is data, not algorithm executor.

93.studyTip: Expert system: Knowledge Base + Inference Engine + Explanation facility.

94.overview:
Expert systems use rule-based reasoning (if-then production rules) mimicking human expert decision-making in narrow domains. ML learns from data; neural nets use weights; GA evolves solutions.

✅ Answer: B — Expert Systems

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. learns patterns from data — not primarily explicit if-then rules.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. rule-based symbolic AI with knowledge base.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. connectionist learning — weighted nodes, not explicit rule bases.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. evolutionary optimization — not if-then expert reasoning.

94.studyTip: Symbolic AI (expert systems) vs Subsymbolic (neural networks, deep learning).

95.overview:
Lifelong/continual learning enables AI systems to adapt incrementally to new data/tasks without catastrophic forgetting — supports evolving environments.

✅ Answer: B — Continuous adaptation to new data

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. goal is maintain/improve performance on new data.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. learn over time as environment changes.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. possible side effect but not the benefit being tested.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. lifelong learning expands applicability — opposite.

95.studyTip: Lifelong learning: adapt without retraining from scratch on all historical data.

96.overview:
Supervised learning trains on labeled examples (input-output pairs). Unsupervised finds structure in unlabeled data (clustering, dimensionality reduction).

✅ Answer: A — Supervised learning uses labeled data, unsupervised does not

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. fundamental ML taxonomy.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. reversed — incorrect.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. speed depends on algorithm/data — not defining difference.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. data requirements vary — not the core distinction.

97.overview:
Decision Trees classify by splitting features on thresholds — interpretable classification algorithm. K-Means clusters unlabeled data; Linear Regression predicts continuous values; PCA reduces dimensions.

✅ Answer: C — Decision Trees

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. unsupervised clustering — not classification of labeled categories.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. predicts continuous numeric output — regression, not classification.
